item.title: The Concise Language Paradigm in left and right hemisphere stroke: a longitudinal source-localized EEG study
item.description:
[预印本] bioRxiv
The mechanisms underlying language recovery after stroke remain poorly understood. Most previous studies have either focused on language comprehension or production and/or relied on hemodynamic measures, with limited complementary electrophysiological evidence. Here, we combined the Concise Language Paradigm (CLaP), assessing comprehension and production, with individualized electroencephalography (EEG) source reconstruction to investigate post-stroke language function and changes in hemispheric dominance over time. In two sessions, we tested stroke-free controls, individuals with left hemisphere (LH) or right hemisphere (RH) stroke. Participants with stroke were assessed two and seven months post-stroke. EEG data were analyzed using event-related potentials and time-frequency representations, followed by source reconstruction based on state-of-the-art individual MRI-derived forward models. Laterality indices were calculated to assess changes in hemispheric dominance between sessions. Behaviorally, the LH group showed low performance at two months followed by overall improvement, whereas the RH group mainly improved in functional communication. EEG activity was significantly modulated by task condition across comprehension and production contrasts. Source-level results in controls were consistent with established language-related networks, serving as regions of interest for the stroke analyses. In the stroke groups, hemispheric dominance differed between LH and RH stroke participants, with LH participants showing systematic shifts from left- to right-hemisphere dominance between sessions, if not already right-hemisphere dominant at two months. Our study provides evidence on comprehension and production performance after stroke using a single paradigm. These findings demonstrate dynamic changes in hemispheric dominance during post-stroke recovery, ultimately highlighting the value of individualized EEG source reconstruction to investigate post-stroke plasticity.

item.title: Unstable word form representations and greater reliance on right hemisphere during word learning in adults with a history of developmental language disorder
item.description:
[预印本] bioRxiv
Impairment in acquiring new vocabulary is a persistent deficit in developmental language disorder (DLD), but its cortical substrates remain unclear. We investigated learning of new words in young adults with DLD and typically developing (TD) control participants using magnetoencephalography (MEG). Participants were exposed to spoken real words and two sets of pseudowords, with shared beginnings, in two MEG sessions. One set of pseudowords was actively trained for three days, paired with fantasy animal pictures. Both groups learned new pseudowords, but adults with DLD recalled fewer items and confused similar sounding pseudowords more often than TD adults. MEG recordings revealed robust left temporal learning effects in both groups, along with left inferior frontal involvement. The DLD group additionally showed stronger right-hemispheric involvement and a significant right temporal learning effect for the newly learned words. Furthermore, only the DLD group showed changes in the left and right temporal responses for the real words after the learning phase, indicating altered lexical access for familiar words after integration of new word forms with overlapping phonology into the mental lexicon. Together, the findings suggest persisting problems in creating and accessing stable and distinctive phonological memory representations for word forms in adults with DLD, along with altered hemispheric balance in processing.

item.title: Intraoperative dorsal cochlear nucleus action potential monitoring in hearing preservation retrosigmoid surgery for vestibular schwannoma: a predictive analysis of short-term hearing outcomes.
item.description:
Journal of neurosurgery
Objective The aim of this study was to evaluate the safety and short-term predictive value of continuous intraoperative monitoring of the dorsal cochlear nucleus action potential (DNAP) using a 4-contact depth electrode during retrosigmoid vestibular schwannoma resection, and to compare its accuracy in predicting postoperative hearing outcomes with that of standard auditory brainstem response (ABR). Methods Adult patients with a preoperative word recognition score (WRS) ≥ 50% who underwent primary retrosigmoid vestibular schwannoma resection were included in this retrospective cohort study. A multimodal monitoring protocol comprising ABR, cochlear nerve action potential mapping, and continuous DNAP monitoring was used. Short-term hearing outcomes were assessed 5-7 days postoperatively based on two criteria: serviceable hearing (American Academy of Otolaryngology-Head and Neck Surgery class A or B) and speech function preservation (WRS ≥ 50%). Multivariate Firth logistic regression and receiver operating characteristic (ROC) curve analyses were performed to identify independent predictors and determine the optimal predictive threshold for DNAP amplitude. In patients with available follow-up, 6-month hearing outcomes were assessed. Results Overall, 153 patients (93 female, mean age 42 years [range 18-68 years]) were included in this analysis, with a mean tumor diameter of 2.2 cm (range 1.5-4.3 cm). Stable baseline DNAP signals were successfully recorded in 80.4% (123/153) of patients compared with 60.8% (93/153) for ABR. No procedure-related complications were attributable to the depth electrode. At 5-7 days postoperatively, serviceable hearing was achieved in 41.2% (63/153) and speech function in 56.2% (86/153) of patients. At the 6-month follow-up, the corresponding rates were 40.9% (56/137) and 56.2% (77/137), respectively, among patients with available audiometric data. In the multivariable analyses, DNAP preservation remained the most consistent independent predictor of both early and 6-month hearing-related outcomes. ROC analysis identified an optimal DNAP residual amplitude ratio cutoff of 0.41 for early postoperative outcomes. In the group with available 6-month follow-up, DNAP retained favorable diagnostic performance and consistently higher sensitivity than that of ABR. Conclusions DNAP monitoring via a 4-contact depth electrode was a safe and reliable technique that provided robust nearly real-time feedback during hearing-preservation vestibular schwannoma surgery. A DNAP residual amplitude ratio > 0.41 was strongly associated with favorable early hearing outcomes, and its diagnostic advantage remained evident at the 6-month follow-up.

item.title: CortexLens: Systematically Decoding Interpretable Visual Patterns from Human Visual Cortex
item.description:
[预印本] PsyArXiv
Understanding how the human brain encodes visual information remains a fundamental challenge in cognitive neuroscience. Sparse dictionary learning (SDL) has recently been applied to fMRI to discover visual features represented in the visual cortex. Existing approaches, however, depend on a vision-language model to identify the feature at discovery, and report limited discovery of the low-level visual features processed in early retinotopic visual regions that play an essential role in human visual cognition. We propose an automatic framework that systematically discovers visual features encoded in the human visual cortex, encompassing both high-level and low-level visual features. The framework decomposes fMRI responses across the full visual hierarchy with Matryoshka sparse autoencoders applied per region of interest, interprets the resulting fMRI activity patterns with a vision-language model, and introduces a set of feature channels to recover the low-level visual features that language-based interpretation fails to capture. On the Natural Scenes Dataset (NSD) and on the Brain Encoder Generated Dataset (BEGD), a separate set of synthesized responses from a transformer brain encoder, the low-level stream recovers thousands of interpretable low-level visual features from early retinotopic visual regions, where prior language-based pipelines report limited discovery. The high-level stream recovers interpretable semantic visual features on both datasets and generalizes to BOLD5000. Our analysis further reveals a systematic confound in language-based interpretation: fMRI activity patterns whose true representation is a low-level visual feature can be misidentified as a semantic visual feature when that feature co-varies with a salient semantic visual feature.

item.title: Human similarity judgments reveal fine-grained representations of dynamic social scenes
item.description:
[预印本] PsyArXiv
How does the human mind organize dynamic social scenes? Existing accounts rely on pre-defined social-affective or action-based taxonomies, yet whether humans use these dimensions to structure their representations of naturalistic social scenes remains unknown. We collected 53,223 human similarity judgments of videos depicting two-person actions and trained a sparse-positive-embedding model to recover the underlying latent dimensions. These learned dimensions explained twice as much variance in similarity judgments as pre-labeled annotations, captured interpretable fine-grained social-event structure (combining information about social relationships and actions), and fractionated broad semantic content (e.g., separating parent-child interactions into caregiving versus affectionate play). The same dimensions also predicted fMRI responses to passively viewed stimuli across visual cortex better than pre-labeled annotations, highlighting their importance beyond similarity judgments. Together, these results suggest that humans represent dynamic social scenes along fine-grained axes not captured by current taxonomies, and offer behaviorally-grounded targets for future studies of social vision.

item.title: The joint modulation of language distance and task demands on the neural mechanisms underlying bilingual lexical processing
item.description:
[预印本] PsyArXiv
Whether bilinguals share the same neural mechanisms for processing their first language (L1) and second language (L2) is a question of broad interest to researchers. Existing studies have accumulated substantial evidence, yet findings remain divergent. The primary sources of inconsistency lie in the language distance between bilinguals' L1 and L2, as well as differences in experimental tasks. Leveraging the advantages of meta-analysis, the present study examined brain activation patterns during L1 and L2 lexical processing in two groups of bilinguals: Chinese–English bilinguals with distant language distance (logographically–alphabetic) and alphabetic–alphabetic bilinguals with close language distance—across different tasks (phonological and semantic). Results showed that in phonological tasks, Chinese–English bilinguals recruited the left inferior parietal lobule/supramarginal gyrus more for L2, a region implicated in orthography-to-phonology conversion; in contrast, alphabetic bilinguals with close language distance shared overlapping neural mechanisms for L1 and L2. In semantic tasks, Chinese–English bilinguals engaged the left middle frontal gyrus and left precuneus more for L1 to support orthography-to-semantics conversion. In contrast, alphabetic bilinguals recruited the left middle temporal gyrus more for L1 for phonology-to-semantics conversion, and engaged language-control regions including the left middle frontal gyrus/inferior frontal gyrus, insula, and inferior parietal lobule more for L2. Further comparisons of brain activation during language-switching tasks between the two bilingual groups also revealed that alphabetic bilinguals with close language distance required greater involvement of executive control regions. Collectively, these findings indicate that the differential brain activation patterns observed when bilinguals process L1 and L2 arise from differences in underlying cognitive processes, jointly driven by language distance and task demands.

item.title: Biophysically constrained learning from healthy neural priors improves motor decoding in pathological cortical networks.
item.description:
Science advances
High-performance brain-computer interfaces (BCIs) rely on stable neural representations, yet brain functional impairments inherently disrupt canonical encoding, creating a fundamental decoding paradox. Conventional data-driven approaches struggle to bridge this gap because of pathological data scarcity and heterogeneity. Here, we propose to leverage healthy neural priors and introduce Pathology-Aware Consensus Training (PACT), a paradigm embedding biophysical constraints into healthy neural recordings to guide neural decoding. In a gesture classification task using high-density electrocorticography from patients with gliomas infiltrating the motor cortex, PACT improved the accuracy by more than 10%, effectively restoring the distorted semantic geometry of motor commands and realigning them with healthy canonical representations (correlation increase: r = 0.66 to r = 0.94). Mechanistically, PACT induced an emergent "inverse weighting" strategy: The model autonomously suppresses high-power pathological noise while reanchoring spatial attention to functional compensatory regions. This study provides a proof of concept for improving decoding in compromised networks by harnessing healthy neural dynamics, laying the theoretical foundation for future BCI deployments in clinical populations.

item.title: The Spectrum within the Spectrum: Neural Heterogeneity in Autism.
item.description:
Behavioural brain research
Autism Spectrum Disorder (ASD) encompasses diverse behavioral, cognitive, and neural profiles that vary widely across individuals. Because diagnosis remains predominantly behavior-based, clinically meaningful within-spectrum differences are often missed. Recent advances in neuroimaging analysis have created opportunities for the identification of distinct neural profiles within ASD. These new avenues provide ways to examine intra-ASD heterogeneity directly, identifying person-specific brain-behavior patterns that group-level comparisons fail to capture. The present systematic review focused on neuroimaging methods (i.e., resting-state fMRI; rs-fMRI, cortical morphology) that emphasized heterogeneity-informed outcomes based on normative modeling, data-driven subtyping, clustering analysis and similar analytic choices. For rs-fMRI, findings showed that differences in connectivity within the default mode and salience networks were linked to social-communication and language impairments, with subtype-specific patterns emerging across samples. In cortical thickness and surface area, studies identified distinct developmental trajectories and individual deviation profiles, with prefrontal and temporal regions often tied to repetitive behaviors and social-communication difficulties. Voxel-based analyses revealed subgroup-specific gray matter alterations, including cerebellar and cortical differences, that aligned with variation in repetitive behaviors and social difficulties. Collectively, this emerging evidence supports the notion that neural heterogeneity in autism is a core feature rather than a limitation. Embracing individual variability can provide crucial insight into the inconsistencies and contradictions of earlier case-control and group-level findings. Moving forward, autism research must prioritize heterogeneity-based methods to establish reproducible subtypes and individualized brain-behavior links.

item.title: The Dutch Mini-Linguistic State Examination (MLSE-NL): findings in Primary Progressive Aphasia (PPA).
item.description:
Journal of neurology
State of the art Changes in speech and language occur as the first symptoms of Primary Progressive Aphasia (PPA). The Mini-Linguistic State Examination (MLSE) is a short speech and language screening test used in the diagnostic process of PPA in English-speaking patients. We adapted the MLSE into Dutch (MLSE-NL) and validated this new version as a diagnostic screening tool in Dutch-speaking patients. Methodology We assessed the MLSE-NL in 90 Dutch-speaking patients with PPA (nonfluent variant PPA (nfvPPA) n = 23, logopenic variant PPA (lvPPA) n = 24, semantic variant PPA (svPPA) n = 32, PPA Not Otherwise Specified (PPA-NOS) n = 11) (mean age: 68.3, 47.8% male) and 276 healthy volunteers (mean age: 56.3, 38.8% male). The MLSE-NL includes subscores in motor speech, phonological structure, semantic knowledge, syntax, and working memory. Group differences were assessed using Kruskal-Wallis tests, with linear models controlling for covariates as confirmatory analyses. Results The MLSE-NL shows significantly lower scores for all PPA variants for total score, ranging from 30 to 96/100 in patients and 83 to 100/100 in controls. The AUC for total score was 0.99 (subdomain AUCs ranged from 0.80 to 0.92). nfvPPA had more motor speech errors than controls, svPPA had more semantic errors, while lvPPA had the most working memory deficits. Syntax errors were frequent in all variants, while phonological deficits were greater in lvPPA and nfvPPA. PPA-NOS had deficits in all domains aside from motor speech. Conclusions The MLSE-NL can successfully discriminate the three canonical variants of PPA and PPA-NOS from controls and captures domain-specific neurolinguistic profiles.

item.title: Individual Differences in Sustained Attention Tune Semantic Abstraction in Neural Encoding of Narratives
item.description:
[预印本] bioRxiv
Neural encoding modeling for narrative comprehension -- using LLM embeddings to predict the temporal dynamics of neural activation -- is widely used to evaluate how well the brain represents certain semantic information. This approach, however, typically collapses semantic representation into a scalar fidelity score aggregated across participants, overlooking potentially rich individual differences and qualitative differences in naturalistic neural representations. In the current study, we addressed this gap by investigating how neural semantic encoding varies across individuals with sustained attention, and whether this difference is qualitative in addition to quantitative. Using fMRI data from 49 participants listening to an audiobook, Le Petit Prince, in English, we trained encoding models with GPT-2 embeddings at varying layers and forecasting lengths. Encoding models trained on high-level embeddings (from the 8th layer of GPT-2) showed significant brain-LLM alignment in 73 of 122 cortical and subcortical ROIs, concentrated in the temporal cortex and the default mode network. Functional connectivity strength in a validated connectome-based predictive model of sustained attention correlated with encoding performance in 18 ROIs, most strongly in the insula and in control and attention networks, with no ROI showing significant opposite relationship. Decomposing semantic information by levels of abstraction showed that the neural signature of sustained attention was selectively associated with a greater proportion of high-level gist information encoded in the frontoparietal and attention networks, while the opposite relationship emerged for proportion of low-level information. Sustained attention scores further predicted stronger predictive coding of upcoming narrative content across multiple networks across the whole brain (control, default mode, salience/ventral attention, limbic, and somatomotor networks). These findings suggest that sustained attention does not uniformly amplify neural semantic encoding, but instead shifts neural representations toward more compressed, gist-level formats that support anticipation of upcoming content. Individual differences in brain-LLM alignment can be a signature of representational strategy rather than noise, with potential utility for cognitive phenotyping.

item.title: Neural correlates of infant dialect discrimination: An fNIRS study.
item.description:
[预印本] PsyArXiv
The present study investigated the neural correlates of infant discrimination of very similar linguistic varieties (Quebecois and Parisian French) using functional Near InfraRed Spectroscopy. In line with previous behavioral and electrophysiological data, there was no evidence that 3-month-olds discriminated the two regional accents, whereas 5-month-olds did, with the locus of discrimination in left anterior perisylvian regions. These neuroimaging results suggest that a developing language network relying crucially on left perisylvian cortices sustains infants’ discrimination of similar linguistic varieties within this early period of infancy.

item.title: A cortical semantic map integrates fractions and integers in the human brain.
item.description:
PLoS biology
How does the human brain represent the meaning of abstract symbols? Some theories postulate the existence of semantic spaces where concepts occupy positions that reflect their conceptual relationships. In the number domain, psychological evidence suggests that integers are represented along a mental number line which, with education, integrates higher-level number concepts such as fractions. To test this hypothesis, we recorded whole-brain 7T fMRI responses to integer and fraction symbols during an active magnitude comparison task designed to engage magnitude processing. Consistent with predictions, we found both behavioral and neural numerical distance effects. Activation vectors in intraparietal, inferior temporal, prefrontal, hippocampal, and parahippocampal cortices formed a two-dimensional semantic space organized by numerical magnitude and domain (fractions versus integers). Gaussian fits revealed a topographic map of numerical preferences in the anterior inferior parietal cortex, common to both domains. Our results suggest that, when educated adults engage in an explicit magnitude comparison task, their brain can construct an ordered representation that integrates fractions and integers, with a topographic organization in the anterior IPS/IPL.

item.title: Multimodal Analysis of Brain Network Abnormalities in Autism Spectrum Disorder: a Graph Neural Network-based Fusion Investigation of EEG and fNIRS.
item.description:
IEEE transactions on bio-medical engineering
Objective This study aimed to identify brain network abnormalities of children with Autism Spectrum Disorder (ASD) by analyzing multimodal neuroimaging data through graph neural networks (GNNs), laying a technical foundation for future machine learning-based neuroimaging analysis. Methods We employed combined electroencephalogram (EEG) and functional near-infrared spectroscopy (fNIRS) to capture brain activity of 58 ASD children and 63 age- and gender-matched typically developing (TD) children. The concurrent EEG and fNIRS data were fused using an enhanced GNN to identify ASD with high accuracy. Key connections and regions of interest (ROIs) were identified for each group, followed by graph theory metrics (e.g., local efficiency) and topological data analysis (TDA) to quantify group differences. Results The proposed GNN model achieved 84% accuracy, outperforming the single-modality approach. Analysis of subgraph created by the model showed that the two groups exhibited different neural patterns in motor-language integration and lateralization, a key basis for GNN models to distinguish between the two groups. Individuals with ASD may also have topological defects such as lower average local efficiency and a lack of high-order structures. Conclusion The proposed framework effectively captures quantitative insights ranging from specific connection-level variations to network-level differences, identifying candidate discriminative connectivity patterns within this cohort. Significance This study establishes a multimodal deep learning framework that identifies candidate discriminative topological signatures from fused EEG-fNIRS data, providing preliminary within-cohort classification evidence and an exploratory topological analysis framework.

item.title: InFACT: Bridging Visual Variance With Semantic Invariance Via Informed Adapter Tuning for Cross-Subject Video Seizure Detection.
item.description:
IEEE journal of biomedical and health informatics
Timely seizure detection is vital for patient intervention. Video-based approaches offer a non-contact, patient-friendly alternative to traditional EEG monitoring. However, their effectiveness is fundamentally hindered by the significant visual variance of seizure behaviors both within and across patients. While existing methods attempt to mitigate this via complex feature extraction, they struggle to eliminate the impact of variance, particularly under drastic appearance shifts caused by complex poses or environmental clutter. Crucially, we observe that although pixel-level appearances fluctuate, the clinical semantics of seizure actions can remain invariant across patients sharing similar semiological patterns. To this end, we propose InFACT (Informed Fusion Adapter with Consistent Text), a dual-branch framework that treats text as a semantic anchor to calibrate visual representations. Specifically, an Informed Fusion Adapter fine-tunes a VideoMAE, a pretrained video masked autoencoder, specializing generic motion priors into seizure-specific pathological patterns under textual guidance. Simultaneously, a Consistency-aware Text Encoder extracts stable behavioral descriptions from a Multimodal Large Language Model, filtering out task-irrelevant visual noise. Furthermore, a cross-modal contrastive learning mechanism aligns divergent visual features with these invariant semantic anchors, ensuring tight clustering of seizure classes regardless of patient identity. Experimental evaluations show that InFACT achieves 86.1% sensitivity, 89.6% specificity on the public SAH-ZU dataset, and 94.3% sensitivity, 96.5% specificity on our in-house FAH-USTC dataset, yielding consistent performance improvements over state-of-the-art methods and proving its robustness against cross-subject variability.

item.title: Neuropharmacology of language: ERP evidence for catecholaminergic modulation of syntactic processing.
item.description:
Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences of the United States of America
A few studies have shown that brain catecholamines are implicated in language comprehension. However, the specific cognitive processes they modulate remain underexplored. We hypothesized that catecholamines enhance the unification of syntactic roles and word meanings into coherent multiword structures. This study combined electroencephalography and psychopharmacology to examine the effects of a catecholaminergic stimulant (methylphenidate) on processing sentences containing local syntactic ambiguities. Methylphenidate amplified the P600 event-related potential effect, which has been linked to the recruitment of cognitive resources for processing sentences with increased syntactic load. The drug's impact on semantic processing was subtler, showing a suggestive attenuation of the N400 effect to ambiguous sentences. Furthermore, the increase in the P600 effect under methylphenidate was most pronounced in participants with lower working memory capacity. This study provides evidence for linking catecholamine activity to syntactic unification in healthy individuals. Elevated catecholamine levels appear to increase the cognitive effort invested in syntactic unification, and to support the dynamic prioritization of syntactic information when contextual demands require it.

item.title: Adult aphasic status epilepticus: A systematic review and patient-level synthesis of clinical phenotypes and multimodal diagnostic evidence.
item.description:
Epilepsy & behavior : E&B
Background Aphasic status epilepticus (ASE) is an uncommon manifestation of focal status epilepticus in which aphasia is the sole or predominant clinical feature. Recognition may be difficult because consciousness can be relatively preserved, convulsive activity may be absent, and the presentation can mimic acute stroke. Objective To characterize diagnostic phenotypes of adult ASE and synthesize clinical, electrographic, and neuroimaging features across published cases. Methods We conducted a systematic review and patient-level synthesis of adult ASE cases. Eligible patients were adjudicated as definite or probable ASE using prespecified criteria. Clinical phenotype, electroencephalographic (EEG) findings, neuroimaging, initial diagnostic impressions, treatment, and language outcomes were extracted. Results Ninety-nine publications contributed 168 adults with ASE, including 89 definite and 79 probable cases. Aphasia was the sole manifestation in 42.9% and predominant in 57.1%, while consciousness was preserved in 78.0%. Ictal EEG activity or electrographic status epilepticus was documented in 53.0%, and 41.7% had supportive epileptiform abnormalities. Among cases with interpretable EEG laterality, 92.7% were left-lateralized. Peri-ictal MRI abnormalities occurred in 41.2% of performed interpretable studies. Among 55 patients with interpretable functional perfusion or metabolic imaging, hyperperfusion was reported in 32. FDG-PET hypermetabolism was treated as a distinct metabolic finding. Stroke or transient ischemic attack was the most frequent reported initial impression (44.2%). Complete language recovery was reported in 77.4% of evaluable patients. Conclusions Published adult ASE cases show a heterogeneous phenotype in which recognition commonly rests on concordance between language disturbance and focal EEG abnormalities, with peri-ictal imaging providing complementary evidence. These findings do not establish diagnostic accuracy of individual features or multimodal combinations.

item.title: Altered Cortico-cerebellar effective connectivity of the Visuo-attentional system is associated with READ1 deletion in developmental dyslexia.
item.description:
NeuroImage. Clinical
Developmental dyslexia (DD) is a heritable neurodevelopmental disorder associated with altered brain connectivity. The influence of genetic risks on cortico-cerebellar effective connectivity (EC) remains unclear. The present study investigates how reading proficiency and the READ1 deletion (READ1d) in the DCDC2 gene modulate visuo-attentional network dynamics. Functional MRI data were acquired in 78 children (DD and typical readers, with/without READ1d) performing a coherent motion detection task. EC within a seven-region visuo-attentional network, including magnocellular, ventral attention, and cerebellar (crus I) regions, was estimated using Dynamic Causal Modelling. Group-level effects were assessed using Parametric Empirical Bayes within a hierarchical Bayesian framework, testing reading proficiency, READ1d status, and their interaction (posterior probability threshold, Pp > 0.95). Reading proficiency was associated with increased cerebellar influence on visual and frontal regions, alongside reduced intra-cortical connectivity within dorsal stream pathways. The presence of READ1d was associated with reduced EC from primary visual and cerebellar regions to magnocellular and ventral attention networks, and increased intra-cortical interactions. The interaction between DD and READ1d revealed further reductions in cortico-cerebellar connectivity and altered network dynamics. Group-level analyses revealed EC differences in cortico-cerebellar pathways, which are reported as exploratory findings. Cortico-cerebellar EC is modulated by both reading proficiency and genetic susceptibility. Altered cerebellar contributions to visuo-attentional processes may represent a potential imaging-genetic signature of dyslexia, warranting replication in independent samples and validation through longitudinal and multimodal approaches.

item.title: Infant gut microbiome neuroactive pathways link to social disadvantage, toddler neurodevelopment, cognitive and behavioural outcomes: a longitudinal cohort study.
item.description:
EBioMedicine
Background Early life is a critical window for co-development of the brain and gut microbiome (GM). Evidence supports a role for the GM in brain development, but longitudinal human data remain limited, particularly regarding the influence of social disadvantage (SD), a powerful determinant of child mental health and neurodevelopment. Here, we examine longitudinal relationships between the GM and neurodevelopmental outcomes over the first three years of life, and the impact of SD on them. Methods We sequenced and analysed stool samples of 187 children, collected at 5 timepoints over 4-36 months of life (MOL; 905 samples) using a whole-metagenome sequencing approach. Associations between GM-derived Gut-Brain Modules (GBM) and neuroactive potential were assessed using generalised linear mixed models, adjusting for covariates. Neurodevelopmental outcomes were evaluated by Bayley-III (cognitive, language, and motor), and neurobehavioural dysregulation and externalising/internalising-behaviour by the Infant-Toddler Social and Emotional Assessment (ITSEA) and Preschool Age Psychiatric Assessment (PAPA). Findings Temporal changes were observed in GBMs, including glutamate/GABA synthesis and degradation pathways, as well as short-chain fatty acids. GM community structure and GBMs were significantly associated with concurrent and later Bayley-III outcomes, most consistently for cognition and language (FDR < 0.10). Several GBMs were associated with both neurobehavioural outcomes and SD, including S-adenosylmethionine (SAM) synthesis, butyrate synthesis, and glutamate and GABA synthesis II (FDR < 0.10). A partial mediating effect between SD and 36 MOL language outcomes was observed using SAM synthesis at 4 MOL (β = -0.042, P = 0.048). Interpretation This longitudinal cohort study of GM neuroactive metabolic capacity across early transitional developmental windows reveals a dynamic pattern of GM-derived neuroactive metabolic pathways and identifies specific pathways associated with later neurodevelopmental (cognitive, language) and neurobehavioural outcomes, even after controlling for important covariates. These pathways are shaped by the socioeconomic status of mothers, starting with in-utero exposure, and GBMs partially mediated this effect. The study identifies microbial pathways associated with both SD and neurodevelopmental outcomes, highlighting potential biological processes that may contribute to neurodevelopmental risk and warrant further investigation. Funding This work was supported by the National Institute of Mental Health, March of Dimes, Children's Discovery Institute, National Institute of Diabetes and Digestive and Kidney Diseases, and National Center for Advancing Translational Sciences.

item.title: SOFEx: A Self-Organized Feature Extraction Approach for Detecting Mild Cognitive Impairment and Alzheimer's Disease using EEG Datasets.
item.description:
Brain topography
Early differentiation of mild cognitive impairment (MCI) from Alzheimer's disease (AD) remains difficult because diagnosis integrates cognitive, imaging, laboratory, and neurological evidence. EEG-based models may provide complementary information, but fixed descriptors can miss signal-specific structure. SOFEx was developed as an adaptive and interpretable EEG feature-engineering framework. The analysis used 1,905 EEG segments from 451 recordings of 168 participants (59 AD, seven MCI, and 102 controls). SOFEx combined self-organized rose pattern extraction, fold-wise feature selection, channel-wise classification, and iterative majority voting. Validation used leave-one-subject-out (LOSO), leave-one-record-out (LORO), and participant-grouped 10-fold cross-validation (CV). Five classifiers were compared under LOSO, and a support vector machine (SVM) was retained. LOSO, used as the primary evaluation of generalization to unseen participants, achieved 84.09% accuracy (95% Wilson CI, 82.38-85.67%), with class-wise recall of 94.47% for AD, 56.59% for controls, and 21.18% for MCI (UAR, 57.41%; macro F1-score, 62.95%). LORO and participant-grouped 10-fold CV achieved 93.65% and 96.38% accuracy, respectively, indicating substantial performance variation across validation schemes. Frontal and parietal electrodes contributed repeatedly to the selected configurations, providing sensor-space information on the signals supporting classification. SOFEx provides an adaptive and interpretable feature-engineering framework for EEG-based classification, combining input-specific pattern selection with sensor-level traceability. Participant-independent evaluation showed high sensitivity for AD, while discrimination of MCI remained more challenging. These findings support the potential of the proposed framework and motivate further validation on larger and independent cohorts to assess its generalizability across clinical settings.

item.title: The Influence of Contralesional Brain Age Gradients on Chronic Stroke Aphasia Severity and Treatment Response.
item.description:
The Journal of neuroscience : the official journal of the Society for Neuroscience
The adult brain follows normative aging trajectories, yet stroke abruptly disrupts this process. Beyond the focal lesion, undamaged regions can deviate from expected aging due to diaschisis or pre-existing vulnerabilities, reflecting tissue health that may constrain recovery. Chronic post-stroke aphasia, a persistent language disorder, shows wide individual variability in severity and treatment response, and these differences are not fully captured by lesion characteristics or demographic factors. Further, prior imaging biomarkers have been difficult to scale because they rely on specialized acquisitions or nonstandardized analytical pipelines. Here, we used a standardized, lifespan-informed brain age model (volBrain) trained on large public datasets to quantify regional deviations from normative aging using only routine structural MRI (T1-weighted). In 188 individuals with chronic stroke (67 female, 121 male), regional aging deviations in the contralesional hemisphere explained aphasia severity beyond lesion volume, lesion location, and basic demographics. In a treated subgroup, baseline brain aging patterns also predicted language gains that persisted 6 months after therapy, indicating prognostic value. By characterizing how individual brains diverge from expected aging, this approach captures variation in tissue integrity that is relevant for both impairment and recovery. This provides a scalable framework that can be integrated across sites and studies, linking normative aging models with post-stroke prognostics and informing precision neurorehabilitation.

item.title: Neurophysiological dynamics related to perception, action, and language in schizophrenia.
item.description:
Science advances
Schizophrenia disrupts both how people perceive the world and how they express and act on their thoughts, yet these symptoms are usually studied separately. Using magnetoencephalography during multisensory and motor tasks, we tested whether reduced event-related beta-band (15 to 30 hertz) modulation, a signal implicated in predictive control, provides a candidate neural marker across these domains. Compared to healthy individuals, patients showed diminished beta changes during sensory processing and movement completion, suggesting reduced flexibility in updating internal models. This neural pattern covaried with audiovisual simultaneity-judgment behavior, disorganized natural speech, and greater clinical severity. These findings suggest that distributed beta modulation may serve as a candidate cross-domain marker associated with perceptual, motor, and language disturbances in schizophrenia, motivating future studies that directly test predictive updating mechanisms.

item.title: Predicting upcoming visual features during eye movements yields scene representations aligned with human visual cortex.
item.description:
Science advances
Natural scenes are complex arrangements of objects, surfaces, and backgrounds. For the brain's visual system to effectively operate, it needs to extract not only what objects are present but also their spatial and semantic relations. We hypothesize that such structures may be learned, in a self-supervised fashion, by exploiting temporal regularities of natural active vision: Each fixation reveals a glimpse that is related to the previous one via co-occurrence and saccade-conditioned spatial regularities. We instantiate this idea with glimpse prediction networks (GPNs), recurrent models trained to predict the embedding of the next glimpse along human-like scanpaths. GPNs are shown to successfully extract complex scene information, including object co-occurrences and spatial object arrangements, and integrate information across glimpses. GPN representations align strongly with human fMRI responses in mid- and higher-level visual cortex and match, often outperform, alternative state-of-the-art ANN models, establishing next-glimpse-prediction as a biologically plausible route toward brain-aligned scene representations.

item.title: Towards semantic brain-computer interfacing: The graded inventory of semantic triggers (GIST) paradigm.
item.description:
Journal of neural engineering
Objective Semantic Brain-Computer Interfaces (sBCIs) aim to decode conceptual information directly from neural activity, enabling more efficient and natural communication for individuals with severe motor impairments. However, existing approaches are often confounded by stimulus-driven perceptual processes and lack a reliable means of tagging the moment of concept formation. We introduce the Graded Inventory of Semantic Triggers (GIST), a novel electroencephalography (EEG) paradigm designed to elicit semantic retrieval from graded verbal clues with precise temporal alignment. Approach: EEG data were recorded from 14 participants performing the GIST task across three semantic categories (food, musical instruments, and body parts). Target neural activity was aligned to each participant's self-reported moment of semantic retrieval (spacebar press), enabling response-locked analysis. Here, we propose a staged framework where the first comprises a Conformer-based encoder trained on pooled data using a hybrid contrastive objective that combines instance-level consistency and cross-participant class alignment with domain-adversarial learning to reduce participant-specific information. In the second stage, the frozen encoder is transferred to a held-out participant whose data played no part in Stage 1, and a support vector machine is calibrated on that participant's own labelled items under a nested leave-one-item-out protocol. Results: Above-chance semantic decoding was achieved in all three pairwise tasks. Mean accuracies were 73.4% (Body vs. Food), 70.7% (Body vs. Music), and 68.2% (Food vs. Music). Participant-level permutation tests were significant in 9/11 participants for Body vs. Food and 8/11 for each of the other tasks (p < 0.05). The pre-response interval at [-1.5s, -0.5s] was the most discriminative. Significance: The GIST paradigm enables controlled elicitation and temporal alignment of semantic processing while reducing perceptual confounds. Combined with cross-participant representation pretraining and participant-specific calibration, the results demonstrate above-chance decoding of semantic categories from EEG in individuals excluded from representation learning, supporting the feasibility of sBCIs.

item.title: The relationship between binocular vision components and visual evoked potentials with reading difficulties in elementary school children.
item.description:
Strabismus
Purpose To assess the relationship between visual function and neural processing with reading/writing defects in elementary school children. Methods This case-control study included 28 boys (8-12 years old) with poor academic performance (study group) and 14 healthy, age-matched controls. All participants underwent a comprehensive optometric evaluation, including visual acuity, refractive error, heterophoria, accommodation and convergence facility, fusional reserves, and monocular Visual evoked potentials (VEPs) using 15- and 60-checkerboard patterns (ISCEV standards). Results No significant differences were found in uncorrected or best-corrected visual acuity between groups (p > .05). However, the study group demonstrated significantly greater hyperopia (+0.07 ± 0.61 D vs. -0.12 ± 0.23 D, p = .025), reduced monocular (6.93 vs. 9.07 cycles/min, p < .001) and binocular (6.04 vs. 8.00 cycles/min, p < .001) accommodative facility, as well as lower vergence facility (6.93 vs. 8.71 cycles/min, p < .001). The study group also exhibited greater exophoria at near (4.61 Δ vs. 2.57 Δ, p < .001) and a reduced distance base-out blur point (10.36 Δ vs. 11.71 Δ, p = .043). VEP measurements revealed a significantly prolonged P100 latency at the 15' check size (112.86 vs. 109.07 ms, p = .043) and higher Fmod values at both 15' (p = .029) and 60' (p = .031) in the study group compared to controls. Conclusion Children with reading difficulties exhibit distinct subclinical visual deficits, particularly in accommodative function, alongside delayed neural processing despite normal visual acuity. Binocular functional assessments and neurophysiological tests should be integrated into assessments of poor academic performance.

item.title: Naturalistic spatial education engages distinct neural processes for mental rotation, cognitive load, and linguistic demands.
item.description:
Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences of the United States of America
Neuroscience studies typically isolate spatial cognition using simplified tasks targeting a single cognitive process. However, during formal spatial education, the brain rarely performs one cognitive operation at a time. Here, we used functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI) to assess neural systems involved in dynamically processing an educational spatial visualization lesson. We quantified lesson content using an instructional-design framework capturing variation in spatial complexity, cognitive load, and verbal density. We then characterized how instructional demands modulated brain function using content-evoked responses, functional connectivity, and network-centrality. Spatial transformations during instruction robustly recruited parietal and premotor regions, which were linearly modulated by spatial complexity. This parietal dominance aligns with theories that these areas encode geometric and quantitative dimensions. In contrast, domain-general frontal activity tracked overall processing demands, and language regions tracked verbal density. Activity also varied with learners' spatial abilities: higher spatial performers showed stronger modulation of parietal and premotor regions as spatial demands increased, and greater domain-general modulation across content types. Thus, the same circuitry representing spatial transformations during instruction also reflects individual variation in spatial cognition. Parietal regions showed the highest centrality and strongest within-network coherence, marking them as the central hub of the system, and distinguishing them from less central and less coherent domain-general regions. Together, the findings reveal how the brain dynamically decomposes complex spatial instruction, preserving parietal-centered spatial processing, while coordinating support from premotor, domain-general, and language systems. These findings begin to reveal how spatial cognition operates within the complexity of formal instruction.

item.title: A New Web-Based Word-Picture Matching Test Reveals Psycholinguistic Effects on Word-Level Reading and Auditory Comprehension in Aphasia.
item.description:
Journal of speech, language, and hearing research : JSLHR
Purpose Word reading comprehension deficits, often measured by word-to-picture matching (WtPM) tasks, are common in aphasia and alexia. To specify the nature of comprehension deficits, WtPM tasks should manipulate psycholinguistic features, have matched written and auditory versions, and provide normed scores measuring speed and accuracy. Here we present a novel web-based WtPM task that meets those needs. We use it to assess word comprehension deficits in left-hemisphere stroke survivors (LHSS). Method We examined scores for the novel auditory and written WtPM task in a normative sample (n = 62) and an LHSS sample (n = 63). Mixed-effects models examined accuracy and response time in both groups, and an analysis of variance compared efficiency between the groups. Correlations compared written WtPM performance and item difficulty to auditory WtPM, written lexical decision, and oral reading. A k -means clustering analysis examined deficit patterns in the LHSS group. Results WtPM performance was modulated by modality, frequency, and regularity and was impaired in the LHSS group. Written WtPM performance and item difficulty were correlated with auditory WtPM and written lexical decision in both groups and with oral reading in the LHSS group. Over half of the LHSS sample had frank deficits on at least one WtPM task. Comprehension deficits in individual LHSS were often modulated by input modality, word frequency, and regularity. Conclusions We present a clinically accessible WtPM task that captures individual patterns of word comprehension impairment in both written and auditory modalities. The use of efficiency scores allows for the assessment of mild impairments that are missed by ceiling effects on currently available tasks. Input modality, frequency, and regularity affect word comprehension as measured by WtPM. Individual stroke survivors present with different combinations of these effects, which may help to identify specific deficits and spared abilities that can guide reading comprehension treatment. Supplemental material https://doi.org/10.23641/asha.33968839.

item.title: Altered language network microstructure links with impaired language function and development in very preterm/very low birth weight born adults.
item.description:
NeuroImage
Premature birth is associated with impaired language function. In premature-born children, language function has been linked with microstructural alterations of the language network.Whether these brain-language associations persist into adulthood remains unclear. We investigated the microstructural properties of major dorsal and ventral language pathways in very preterm/very low birth weight (VPT/VLBW) adults and their associations with language performance in adulthood and childhood. Sixty-three VPT/VLBW and eighty full-term-born adults (mean age 26.8 years) underwent diffusion-weighted imaging and language assessment. The arcuate fasciculus, superior longitudinal fasciculus, uncinate fasciculus and inferior fronto-occipital fasciculus were reconstructed using probabilistic tractography from which fractional anisotropy (FA) and mean diffusivity (MD) measures were extracted. Adult language function was assessed via the Regensburg word fluency test, rapid automatized naming and verbal IQ; childhood language was assessed at the mean age of 8 using the Kaufman Assessment Battery for children. We observed altered language network microstructure in VPT/VLBW participants, illustrated by lower FA and higher MD in the SLF and UF. These microstructural alterations were associated with language function in adulthood, but also with language development in childhood. We found that the association between tract microstructure and language abilities differed between groups. Our results demonstrate altered language network microstructure in premature born adults, which links with impaired language function and development. These findings extend previous work by comprehensively characterizing the adult dorsal and ventral language network and relating its microstructural properties to language function across development. The selective follow-up sample may limit generalizability to the broader VPT/VLBW population.

item.title: Artificial intelligence for symptom assessment and patient-reported outcomes in neuro-oncology.
item.description:
Journal of neuro-oncology
Purpose Patient-reported outcomes (PROs) are critical tools for measuring how patients experience their illness and treatment. Neuropsychiatric symptoms, headaches, seizures, and neurological deficits evolve over time and impact quality of life. In this narrative review, we summarize current literature on PROs in neuro-oncology, extant artificial intelligence (AI) tools for PRO analysis, considerations for real-world application, and ethical implications. Methods We searched PubMed/MEDLINE, Embase, and Google Scholar for English-language articles published from January 2015 through April 2026, supplemented by reference-list reviews. Four themes were agreed upon, and authors were assigned to each theme. Authors conducted a literature review, selected articles, and synthesized the information under each of these themes. An initial 78 articles were narrowed down to 53 confirming eligibility if they reported PRO or symptom data in people with brain tumors or computational/AI methods were applied to PRO or symptom monitoring in oncology. Article selection was verified by two senior authors (L.V.Y, A.S.). Older, foundational studies were retained where they remain the primary evidence. Results The growing volume and complexity of PRO data present challenges for traditional analysis methods. Integrating AI, including machine learning (ML) and large language models (LLMs), may help model longitudinal symptom trajectories to predict deterioration, extract symptoms from free-text clinical notes, and embed outputs in clinical decision support tools. Autonomy, informed consent, data security, bias, access, transparency and accountability should be considered. Conclusion Successful translation will require interpretable, electronic health record-integrated, bias-mitigating tools that allow for actionable insights and preserve patient consent, privacy, and autonomy in this highly vulnerable population. Clinical trial number Not applicable.

item.title: Neurotransmitter-defined cerebral vulnerability patterns in frontotemporal lobar degeneration (FTLD).
item.description:
Journal of neurology
Background Frontotemporal dementia syndromes encompass a genetically, clinically and radiologically heterogeneous set of conditions with distinctive clinical and imaging characteristics. The main FTD phenotypes exhibit strikingly different disease burden patterns with a predilection to specific brain regions and relative sparing of others. The apparent selectivity of cerebral involvement in FTD has not been fully elucidated. Methods A prospective neuroimaging study has been undertaken with a uniform imaging protocol to characterise atrophy patterns in ALS-FTD, behavioural variant FTD, nonfluent variant primary progressive aphasia, and semantic variant primary progressive aphasia and evaluate associations with physiological neurotransmitter receptor expression maps. Anatomical correlations between focal volume loss and a large panel of neurotransmitters were systematically evaluated and associations ranked. Results Associations were noted with GABAergic, opioid, cannabinoid, microglial and acetylcholine systems in ALSFTD-C9NEG. Correlations were observed with opioid, glutaminergic, and synaptic vesicle glycoprotein 2A receptor populations in ALSFTD-C9POS. Atrophy in bvFTD showed predilection to serotonergic, glutaminergic, opioid, GABAergic and cannabinoid circuits. Volume loss in nfvPPA colocalised with GABAergic, opioid, microglial, serotonergic, cannabinoid, acetylcholine, glutaminergic and dopaminergic networks. A multitude of neurotransmitter populations are implicated in svPPA including opioid, serotonergic, GABAergic, dopaminergic, and microglial systems. Discussion The distinctive neuroimaging signatures of FTD phenotypes exhibit spatial associations with physiological neurotransmitter receptor density maps. The propensity of atrophy to specific brain regions in FTD subtypes may be defined by neurotransmitter populations. Our findings indirectly support the notion of neurotransmitter-system defined connectivity-based disease propagation in FTD.

item.title: Mapping the brain signature of dyslexia risk onto histamine, acetylcholine and glutamate receptor systems
item.description:
[预印本] medRxiv
The brain differences of dyslexia are well described and its genetic risk is now measurable; the brain systems that connect the two are unknown. That link decides which measures complement one another in early identification and which systems intervention research should examine. Here we compared large-scale polygenic score maps of brain structure in dyslexia with normative maps of brain neurotransmitter systems. The structural signature of genetic liability aligned with the cortical distribution of neurotransmitter systems. The strongest and most consistent alignment appeared for the histamine H3 receptor, the vesicular acetylcholine transporter (VAChT) and the N-methyl-D-aspartate (NMDA) glutamate receptor. The alignment was most pronounced in cingulate, medial and superior frontal cortex and the paracentral lobule. The H3 alignment held after adjustment for cortical position and for metabolic and cognitive reference maps. Once the component common to all nineteen maps and position were removed together, no individual system remained significant, while the shared component itself aligned with liability. The signature therefore follows the topography these systems share. In 169 children, per-person alignment with the H3 map related to reading skill with the opposite sign to liability. To our knowledge, this is the first study to relate the structural signature of genetic liability for dyslexia to normative maps of neurotransmitter receptor and transporter density. It places that signature within the shared geography of the systems that set attention, arousal and synaptic plasticity during learning, and gives the genetics of dyslexia a testable biological axis.

item.title: Synergistic modulation of the dorsolateral prefrontal cortex and precuneus enhances cognitive recovery in mild cognitive impairment: A multimodal neuroimaging study.
item.description:
Neural regeneration research
Abstract Repetitive transcranial magnetic stimulation is a promising intervention for mild cognitive impairment; however, conventional single-site stimulation protocols are often incapable of addressing the complex pathological network alterations underlying the condition. This study investigated the clinical efficacy and neurobiological modulatory mechanisms of multisite versus single-site repetitive transcranial magnetic stimulation in patients with mild cognitive impairment. A total of 101 patients with mild cognitive impairment completed a 10-day repetitive transcranial magnetic stimulation intervention and were analyzed in two cohorts: a single-site group receiving stimulation over the left dorsolateral prefrontal cortex (n = 50) and a multi-site group receiving sequential stimulation over the left dorsolateral prefrontal cortex and precuneus (n = 51). The multi-site group demonstrated significantly greater enhancements in global cognition [Mini-Mental State Examination: group×time interaction F(99) = 25.08, P < 0.001; Montreal Cognitive Assessment: F(99) = 6.17, P = 0.015], memory [Auditory Verbal Learning Test-immediate recall: F(99) = 6.03, P = 0.016], and language (Verbal Fluency Test, Animal Fluency Test: F(99) = 8.13, P = 0.005) compared with the single-site group. Neuroimaging analyses revealed that multi-site repetitive transcranial magnetic stimulation induced robust structural and functional alterations across broader cognitionrelated regions and networks. Specifically, the multi-site protocol significantly increased gray matter volume in the left parahippocampal gyrus and large-scale networks (e.g., default mode network, executive control network), while modulating amplitude of low-frequency fluctuation and regional homogeneity in core memory and executive regions, including the precuneus, hippocampus, parahippocampal gyrus, and middle frontal gyrus. Additionally, multi-site stimulation drove more extensive functional connectivity alterations within the left parahippocampal network. Crucially, these specific neuroimaging alterations significantly correlated with behavioral improvements in memory, language, and global cognitive scores. Multi-site repetitive transcranial magnetic stimulation targeting the left dorsolateral prefrontal cortex and precuneus yields superior cognitive improvements in mild cognitive impairment compared with conventional single-site stimulation. This enhanced efficacy is underpinned by the robust modulation of structural integrity, spontaneous neural activity, and functional connectivity within core cognitive brain networks. These mechanisms reflect repetitive transcranial magnetic stimulation-induced synaptic plasticity and neurovascular coupling, driving network-level neural repair and providing a mechanistic rationale for optimized, connectivity-based neuromodulation in the early intervention of Alzheimer's disease.

item.title: The Neural Correlates of Implicit Emotion Regulation through Affect Labeling as Reflected in EEG
item.description:
[预印本] PsyArXiv
Affect labeling reduces emotional responses during and immediately after use, but evidence for lasting regulatory effects remains mixed. While there is no experiential evidence for lasting effects, psychophysiological studies do hint at a longer-lasting impact. However, neuroimaging research has mainly compared affect labeling with affect matching. Although both involve emotional processing, affect labeling additionally engages linguistic processing. Thus, it remains unclear whether observed neural differences reflect emotion-focused labeling or mere linguistic processing, and whether such effects endure over time. We recorded EEG to examine the effects of affect labeling on negative emotion across two re-exposure phases: immediate and after a short interval (15 minutes). Affect labeling (emotion-specific words) was compared with affect matching (emotion-focused perceptual processing) and feature labeling (linguistic processing without emotional content), allowing us to dissociate emotional and linguistic components. Event-related potentials and EEG oscillatory activity were analyzed in both phases, with pre-intervention neural responses included as baseline. Robust emotion-related neural activity was observed. Negative (vs. neutral) stimuli elicited increased late positive potential (LPP) amplitudes, enhanced fronto-central-parietal theta power, and greater right-hemispheric alpha activity. However, LPP, theta-, and alpha-band power did not show effects of affect labeling compared to the control conditions. Thus, the present findings provide no evidence for a lasting labeling effect. Because we focused on re-exposure, we may have missed potential regulatory effects during the intervention itself. Future research should further identify factors that influence the effectiveness of labeling and clarify when this implicit emotion regulation pathway is engaged.

item.title: Humanizing AI-generated exemplars: Human-source framing facilitates group creative ideation
item.description:
[预印本] PsyArXiv
Artificial intelligence (AI)-generated creative exemplars are increasingly used as scalable digital instructional resources in creativity education. However, it remains unclear whether labeling identical exemplars as human- or AI-generated shapes how learners engage in group creative activities. We tested this possibility in 113 dyads using an fNIRS hyperscanning group creative ideation paradigm. Dyads completed creative ideation tasks before, during, and after exemplar-stimulation. During stimulation, the human- and AI-attribution groups received identical exemplars labeled as produced by human or AI, whereas the control group received no exemplar. Human attribution increased idea uniqueness during stimulation relative to both the other phases and the AI-attribution and control groups. AI attribution temporarily increased switching among ideation pathways. Neither behavioral effect persisted after exemplar withdrawal. The two attribution groups did not differ in exemplar-category overlap or nearest-exemplar semantic distance, but human-attribution dyads rated the exemplars as more helpful. Human attribution also increased interbrain synchronization (IBS) in bilateral premotor and supplementary motor cortices during stimulation, whereas AI attribution was associated with decreased IBS in the left supramarginal gyrus and right frontopolar cortex from pre- to post-stimulation. Thus, exemplar-source attribution shapes the process and outcome of group creative ideation, revealing an important social-contextual factor in AI-supported creativity education.

item.title: A Longitudinal Investigation of Cannabis Use on Adolescent Neurocognitive Development in the ABCD Study®
item.description:
[预印本] PsyArXiv
Objective. Evidence pertaining to the effect of adolescent cannabis use on neurocognitive development has been mixed, with recent reports highlighting the limitations of existing findings. By leveraging the Adolescent Brain Cognitive Development (ABCD) Study® sample, the present study addresses previous methodological constraints to clarify cannabis’s potential effect on cognitive development.Methods. Youth (N=4,191) performed neurocognitive tasks during their baseline (age ~10) and Year 6 (age ~16) follow-up assessments. Domains included overall cognitive function (crystallized/fluid), memory, executive functioning, processing speed, reward sensitivity, and language skills. Lifetime, cumulative cannabis use was divided along a median split to account for skewed data, resulting in no, low (≤5 cannabis use occasions; average=1.8), and high use (>5 use occasions; average=256) groups. Initial models (Bonferroni corrected, n=19) compared Year 6 follow-up cognitive performance between groups while controlling for baseline performance, sex, and age. Sensitivity analyses incorporated 1) socioeconomic status (SES), 2) additional substance use, and 3) SES and additional substance use.Results. Cannabis use during early adolescence was significantly related (adj. p<0.05) to worse crystallized cognitive function (β=[-0.23,-0.21]), memory (β=[-0.35,-0.17]), and language skills (β=[-0.26,-0.13]). Cannabis effects remained generally consistent after controlling for SES alone. After controlling for additional substance use, the unique effect of cannabis use was no longer statistically significant.Conclusions. The present study highlights that cannabis likely has an overall negative effect on neurocognitive development; while present over and above SES, this effect may not be substance specific. Future work aims to disentangle the shared effect of these relationships.

item.title: Plasticity in Human Brain Language Areas After Stroke: What Can the Right Hemisphere Do?
item.description:
The Neuroscientist : a review journal bringing neurobiology, neurology and psychiatry
Among the most devastating effects stroke can have on the lives of survivors and those around them are language production and comprehension impairments. The most notable of them - often given the joint diagnostic label of "aphasia" despite their heterogeneity and dissociability - are associated with damage to the brain's left hemisphere, which, in large part for this reason, is considered the "language-dominant" hemisphere. However, the right hemisphere's contribution to language should not be underestimated and may in fact be key to understanding the possibilities and limitations of neuroplasticity for supporting language recovery after stroke. Thus, in this review, we focus on the role of the right hemisphere in supporting human language function, in the neurologically healthy brain and after stroke. We discuss the remarkable capability of the right hemisphere to support normal language abilities after a large left-hemisphere stroke early in life, the more limited capacity for right-hemisphere language support after left-hemisphere stroke in adulthood, and potential interactions between typically left-hemisphere dominant "core" language functions with language functions typically thought to be right-hemisphere dominant, such as emotional prosody. We conclude by highlighting gaps in current knowledge and suggesting areas for future research.

item.title: The effect of text-picture consistency on memory integration in college students: Evidence from ERPs.
item.description:
The British journal of educational psychology
Background In multimedia learning, individuals often need to integrate textual and visual information. The neural mechanisms underlying how consistency between text and pictures affects memory integration remain unclear. Aim To examine the effect of text-picture consistency on memory integration in college students and to determine the processing time at which this effect occurs. Sample Totally 28 Chinese college students (nfemale = 20, nmale = 8; Mage = 21.64 ± 2.30) participated in this experiment. Methods An adapted pictorial demonstration paradigm was employed. Participants sequentially learned two pairs of text-picture stem facts (consistent vs. inconsistent), separated by an interval, followed by a recognition test for stem and integrated facts. Behavioural and event-related potential (ERP) data were recorded simultaneously. Results Under the text-picture consistency condition, college students showed significantly better memory integration performance than under the inconsistency condition (58% vs. 48%). EEG results showed that the text-picture inconsistency condition (i.e., the picture and text within a single stem fact were semantically mismatched) elicited a larger P600 wave (500-800 ms) than the text-picture consistency condition, suggesting that text-picture inconsistency primarily induces conflict and integration difficulties during late cognitive processing. No significant differences were observed in the early N400 component. Conclusion Text-picture consistency facilitates memory integration primarily during late processing, aligning with cognitive theories of multimedia learning. Educationally, it serves as a key quality indicator for multimedia material design. Instructors should prioritize semantic alignment and assess knowledge integration during evaluation.

item.title: Delineating neural contributions to electroencephalogram-based speech decoding.
item.description:
Journal of neural engineering
Objective . Speech Brain-computer interfaces (BCIs) have emerged as a pivotal technology in facilitating communication for individuals with speech impairments. Utilizing electroencephalography (EEG) for noninvasive speech BCIs offers an accessible and affordable solution, potentially benefiting a broader audience. However, EEG-based speech decoding remains controversial especially for overt speech, due to difficulties in separating speech-related neural activities from myoelectric potential artifacts generated during articulation. Moreover, because paradigms for collecting covert speech data are inherently less scalable than those for overt speech, whether the neural dynamics underlying EEG-based decoding of overt speech are also present during covert speech remains an open and practically important question. Approach . Here we aim to delineate the extent of the neural contributions to EEG-based speech decoding, and the degree to which the underlying neural dynamics are shared across overt and covert speech, by employing Explainable AI techniques to a convolutional neural network predicting spoken words based on signals obtained by ultra-high-density (uhd)-EEG. Main results . We found that electrode-wise contributions to the decoding cannot be explained by their mutual information with electromyography (EMG). Furthermore, contributing periods of speech to EEG-based decoding are distinct from those to decoding solely relying on EMG. In contrast, there are significant overlaps in signal timings contributing to EEG-based decoding, regardless of vocal conditions such as overt or covert speech. Notably, the denoising process successfully enhanced the decoding contribution from electrodes within speech-related brain areas for all speech conditions. Significance

item.title: The spatial extent of fast ripples is associated with cognitive and language deficits in children with focal epilepsy: An exploratory SEEG study.
item.description:
Epilepsy & behavior : E&B
Objective To determine if the spatial extent of interictal fast ripples in focal epilepsy patients is associated with brain dysfunction. Methods Thirty pediatric focal epilepsy patients who underwent SEEG investigation had their cognitive and language deficits assessed in scales of 0 to 4. Fast ripples (250-500 Hz), ripples (80-250 Hz), and IEDs were automatically detected in 10 min during NREM sleep. We fitted linear models to the relationship between the cognitive deficit scale and the spatial spread of the interictal neurophysiologic events (number of channels with rate of events > 10 % of maximum rate). For the language deficit, we computed the Spearman correlation between the median rate of events in all brain regions and the deficit scale. Results Cognitive deficit scale was significantly associated with the number of channels with fast ripples (p = 0.049), not so with ripples (p = 0.31), IEDs (p = 0.31). The potential confound of number of explored channels did not improve the fitting of the models. Language deficits were not correlated with the number of channels showing interictal events. However, from all brain regions the most statistically significant correlations (p < 0.01) were between median fast ripple rates in the left and right pars opercularis and triangularis of the inferior frontal gyrus (Broca's area and its contralateral counterpart) with r = 0.66, p = 0.003 (18 patients), in the superior temporal gyrus in the language dominant hemisphere with r = 0.72, p = 0.005 (13 patients), and the dominant basal temporal region with r = 0.79, p = 0.006 (10 patients). Median rates of IEDs and ripples exhibited lower correlation with language deficits in these regions. Conclusion Widespread fast ripples are associated with increased cognitive deficits, and language deficiencies are correlated with fast ripple rates in brain regions associated with language. The extent of fast-ripple activity was associated with cognitive deficit severity in this cohort, whereas the corresponding associations for ripples and IEDs did not reach statistical significance.

item.title: Resting-state fMRI biomarkers of surgical outcome in temporal lobe epilepsy: Network reorganization, rsfMRI-based prediction models, and cognition - A systematic review.
item.description:
Neuroscience and biobehavioral reviews
Temporal lobe epilepsy (TLE) is a network disorder extending beyond the structurally defined epileptogenic zone. Resting-state functional MRI (rsfMRI) may provide information on brain network alterations relevant to seizure outcome and cognitive risk after epilepsy surgery. We reviewed rsfMRI studies in TLE surgical cohorts to evaluate postoperative network changes, preoperative predictors of seizure outcome, and associations between functional connectivity and cognition. This systematic review followed PRISMA guidelines and was registered in PROSPERO. Fifteen studies were included, comprising 474 TLE patients who underwent resective epilepsy surgery and had at least 1 year of follow-up. Studies were reviewed for patient population, surgery, rsfMRI methodology, networks or regions, outcome definition, postoperative network changes, and cognitive assessments. Despite heterogeneity in patient selection, surgery, rsfMRI analysis, and outcome definition, studies consistently reported reduced DMN-related connectivity in TLE compared with healthy controls. Postoperative functional connectivity in seizure-free patients shifted toward healthy controls patterns in few studies. Preoperative rsfMRI-based prediction models showed promising accuracy for predicting seizure outcome but were generally developed in small cohorts and lacked external validation. Evidence relating rsfMRI to cognition was limited, but implicated thalamic, ascending reticular activating system, and thalamo-occipital connectivity in attention, language, and executive functions. RsfMRI is a promising research biomarker for network-level risk stratification in TLE surgery, particularly for seizure outcome prediction and postoperative network reorganization. Current evidence remains insufficient for clinical implementation. Future studies require larger homogeneous multicenter cohorts, standardized acquisition and preprocessing, consistent outcome definitions, systematic postoperative rsfMRI, neuropsychological assessment, and external validation of prediction models.

item.title: Clinical referral text overrides MRI evidence in multimodal large language models: glioma versus brain abscess
item.description:
[预印本] medRxiv
Objectives To determine how strongly clinical referral text, rather than image content, drives the decisions of multimodal large language models (LLMs) differentiating glioma from brain abscess on MRI. Materials and methods This retrospective single-center study included 60 contrast-enhanced T1-weighted brain MRI examinations (30 gliomas, 30 abscesses; reference-standard diagnosis). One axial slice per case was paired with five referral texts (explicitly inflammatory to explicitly tumor-suggestive) under three prompt instructions and submitted 20 times each to GPT-4o, Claude Sonnet 5, Gemini 3.5 Flash, and Qwen 3.6 (72,000 answers). The primary outcome was the text-driven span (difference in tumor-call frequency between explicit inflammatory and explicit tumor text). Two blinded radiologists classified the images without text; sensitivity, specificity, and accuracy were compared descriptively. Results Patients (29 women) had a mean age of 55.8 ± 16.4 years. With neutral text, models answered tumor in 45–67% of queries (specificity, 0.38–0.78), versus 52% and 60% for radiologists (specificity, 0.77 and 0.63). The text-driven span was 0.79–1.00 ( p < 0.001 for all models), whereas confirmed gliomas and abscesses differed by only 0.01–0.10 in three models and 0.25 in Gemini 3.5 Flash. Subtle wording produced at least 83% of the span in three models. An instruction to ignore the text reduced the span to 0.48–0.70 in three models and to 0.04 in Gemini 3.5 Flash, partly through reversion to a tumor default. Model accuracy was 0.52–0.73 versus 0.78 and 0.73 for radiologists. Conclusion Multimodal LLMs deferred to referral text over imaging evidence in differentiating glioma from brain abscess, and prompt instructions did not reliably correct this. Key Points Question Multimodal large language models receive images together with clinical referral text, but how strongly the text rather than the image determines their diagnosis is unknown. Findings Changing only the referral text largely reversed the glioma-versus-abscess decision for identical MRI images in four models; instructions to ignore the text reduced this inconsistently. Clinical relevance Before clinical use, multimodal large language models require model- and task-specific testing of their susceptibility to referral text, because instructing them to prioritize the image is not a dependable safeguard against text-driven misdiagnosis.
